review_text:
I was invited to the soft opening by a friend of friend of the owner's family.  I was very impressed upon arrival with the modern ambiance and group style seating which is a nice change of pace in NYC where it is often hard to bring a good sized group.  The wait staff also gets a lot of points for being kind and attentive.  I had the opportunity to speak with owners who gave me a brief history of the restaurant and its culinary objectives.  While I hope the restaurant becomes popular, I also hope that the owners do not lose that personal touch I felt while I was there.  I also give them credit for creating a very elegant menu with pictures which can be helpful for those who often do not eat Thai food.
The food itself was amazing.  Well cooked, and well presented.  I went with two other dinners and between us we split plates of fried chicken thighs, duck salad, pork with basil, and rice noodles.  There was nothing we tried that I did not like.  My only criticisms come on the size of the potions and size of the rice side.  The portions are larger than Tapas, but you would need to order more than one for a filling meal.  I also think that they would do well to provide you sides of rice with your meal.  The rice side offered is kind of small and some of the food can be spicy, which is great if you like spice, but if you are a spice wimp like me having that rice could be important.

Best papaya salad I've ever had outside of Thailand. That and the other dishes are excellent as well.

We generally use papaya salad as the barometer of a Thai restaurant. After trying it here, you'll realize that what you've had at other restaurnts bears little resemblance to the real thing. This is good authentic Issan food, a nice change from the standard curry and noodle Thai restaurant, but even more fresh and delicious. You will not be dissapointed.

All in all, a wonderful addition to the neighborhood. Friendly staff, affordable prices, and delicious food.  So good in fact that I was inspired to register on yelp and post my first review.

Dish reccomendations: Papaya salad with crab, roast pork, roast beef.

Came here was a friend last night. He had read an article that said the place was brand new and getting rave reviews so we decided to check it out. I wasn't really sure what to expect but was very pleasantly surprised! The food was fantastic! The minced duck salad was a perfect dish. So many fresh herbs and spices! The chef obviously pays close attention to the quality of the ingredients. I also had the sun dried beef which was which was very flavorful too. My friend ordered the grilled beef skewers and the taro in condensed Milk for dessert, both of which I would highly recommend. 

Many of the dishes on the menu will seem unfamiliar to people who haven't eaten a lot of Isan cuisine, making it a little hard to narrow down your options. But the way they have set up the menu helps a lot. There are plenty of pictures and descriptions to help guide you through deciding what to order. Everything is great for sharing so I'd bring a friend or two so you can try several different dishes. Just keep in mind that the dishes come in fairly small portions so you will probably need to order more than one thing per person or you may not feel full. 

My only complaint was that the service could have been a bit more attentive, but they were very friendly and were willing to make suggestions and answer any questions we had about the menu. I'm sure they'll work out the kinks eventually. Overall I think this place is going to be very successful and I definitely plan on coming back!

Went in a week ago.  The only reason that this place is getting 3 stars is because the food is pretty damn good.  The service was beyond bad.  We ordered a starter to share, two entrees, and two drinks.  The drinks came after two of the dishes - the waitress forgot the starter.  Um so annoying to want a pre dinner cocktail and have to drink it with the meal.  The food was really good though.  Love the coconut rice. 

Because the service sucked, I decided to take out.  Waited in the restaurant for my food - 5 minutes late, fine.  Then when I got home- wrong order!  UGH.  Was too exhausted to bring back or even complain so BF and I ate it.  Blah.  

Get your act together please.  It could be so much better.  The food is good.

Went on a Saturday night with two friends and we had a great time! The food is absolutely fantastic... definitely a notch up from your typical Thai food. They said the wait was around 30 minutes, and we ended up waiting almost an hour, but it was worth it. Will absolutely go again.

Great to see another authentic Issan Thai restaurant in the East Village (and Manhattan in general). However, sadly, the food is just mediocre and you can actually get better quality and value for your money at Zabb Elee (also in the East Village) or just go out to the number of Issan restaurants in Queens.

The standout dish was the Raw Shrimp Sashimi. Very similar to what I had when I was in Thailand. Very spicy too!

The Som Tum with land crab was downright awful, which was disappointing since it was one of their "Specialty" dishes. Really salty and bad, fishy after-taste. Maybe their standard Som Tum is better? 

The Laab Moo (pork) was OK, but the fish sauce they used was rather salty. 

The Fried Chicken was tasty, but their wasn't much meat on the plate. Good for one person, but hard to share with two.

Finally, we had the Thai Sausage. Decent dish, but had better elsewhere.

Super delicious meal tonight. Grilled and fried dishes were great, somtum was yummy. Overall really great eats, and looking forward to going back. 

Make sure you try the coconut glazed beef and the larb.

So this is one of the newer entries into the Asian cuisine world. It's a little different and it's not your typical Thai place with all the curries. But rather it's a style of Thai food that has it's origins from the Northeastern part of Thailand.  It uses tons of fresh ingredients, such as peppers and papaya. A lot of their main dishes are salads with meat.  

The decor was very nice and modern, very welcoming. And has a beer house type feeling with the benches for their big tables.  Nice and dimly lit atmosphere.  It is a welcomed addition to the grunge feeling of Alphabet City/East Village/Lower East Side restaurants.

The food itself is actually pretty good. I had the garlic beef rice dish. I found it full of flavor and has a more home cooking style than what you would normally find at other Thai places.  Simple, meat and rice dish. Nothing else. But one thing I hope they tone down a little bit in the future before I consider going again is their saltiness. The dishes were very salty for my tastes. And I love salty foods.

If you are looking for something new. Give it a try.

Pretty standard Thai place in terms of decor and service, although you can tell the food is very authentic. The portions aren't amazing, but the food is very flavorful.

Had the Larb Moo (which is minced pork salad) and the Pad See Eil. Pretty killer flavors and they didn't overpower the Larb Moo with spice. The Pad See Eil was a bit different and had more vegetables and shrimp than actual noodles, which was okay. Might need a few more carbs in that dish. Heh.

The fried chicken thigh was also delicious. Again, we didn't really go quite that adventurous from the usual Thai dishes, but everything we had was very well done.

Overall, while the food was definitely well done and authentic, the feel of the place and the service wasn't mind-blowing, and if you are in the mood for something other than the run-of-the-mill pad thai or pad see eil, this is definitely worth trying.

Lunch specials $10-$12!

We sampled both lunch sets and found both to be very good. The $12 lunch special comes with Spicy Papaya Salad and Deep-Fried Chicken Thigh w/ Sticky Rice. The sticky rice was amazing and tasted really good with the deep-fried chicken, which was very juicy and succulent. The papaya salad, though, was super super super spicy! Both of us couldn't eat more than 2 bites. 

We also tried $10 lunch special - I opted for the Fried Garlic Pork with Jasmine Rice. Pop the egg, let it soak into the rice and eat with a piece of pork. It is heavenly! The flavors are like a small punch in the face. It also comes with a pork cartilage soup, which was also super spicy!! Too spicy!! 

We also ordered a Fried Sticky Rice on the side and it was really good. The rice was very fragrant and had a sweet, yet salty, taste to it. So so so good! It is a must try!

Yesterday I went to this place for brunch the waitress seems not so happy it was just like she doesn't have a service mind in herself. At that time wasn't busy at all so I ordered Tum Saur Der ,Tum Kai Kem and Kao kluk kapi I did tell her not to salty n I need both of the papaya salad to be sweet n sour but idk if she listened, when the food being served it was salty I just don't get it why it was only our table how come the service was that bad ? Was she listened to what I ordered? If it was busy I would understand but this really unacceptable. I went there a couple time b4 n kinda like this place but since yesterday I might have changed my mind (normally I'm going there for dinner it was nice n staff was nice) maybe it wast unlucky day to met the attitude face server :/

Menu is quiet massive, tons of selections. We ordered quite a few dishes and everything was delicious.  

My favorite was pork skewer on a stick with skinny noodles on the side. It was tender and perfectly seasoned. 

I thought I could handle spicy papaya salad but next time will only ask for 1 chili 

Pad Thai was great too, served with crab meat. 

Had another pork dish with fried minced garlic sprinkled in top, delicious!!! 

Will definitely come back and try other items on the menu.

Oh and they are quite creative with cocktail so definitely check that out too.

I was super excited to try this place. I was in Thailand earlier this year and while I had a good amount of Thai street food, I wasn't able to try as many Isan Thai dishes while I was there. 

Between three of us, we split the Tum Thai Kai Kem (papaya salad w/ salted egg), Por Pla Larb Moo (spicy pork spring rolls), Larb Pla Dook Yang (catfish larb), and Larb Moo (pork larb). We also ordered one of the soups, but I can't remember which.

The spicy pork spring rolls were actually very good. I thought they would be boring run of the mill spring rolls, but the seasoning was great. Even the vegetarian in our group had a bite and loved it!

Papaya salad w/ salted egg was divine. My friend worked in Bangkok for 4 years and she mentioned that she hasn't been able to get this specific papaya salad anywhere else in the city (well anywhere where it tasted right in any case). The spicy, cold papaya combined with the salty warm egg was so so yummy.

The two larbs were great. I think we actually preferred the catfish larb. It seemed to absorb the flavors better and have a hint of sweetness and caramelization. The combination of flavors  was perfect!

I highly recommend trying this place out. Note that the best dishes here are the ones that are spicy and sour as those are characteristics of Isan cuisine. The noodle/curry type of dishes at other Thai restaurants aren't really the strengths as they aren't really Isan cuisine.

This place changes its name practically every year and I always get suckered into wistfully thinking it will not be as bad as before. Once when I asked why the place needs the face lift, a staff told me that the owner thinks the feng shui or luck would be better. I don't know much about that sort of thing but if I were him/her, I would to put more effort into producing better food and less on changing the design and decor on a regular basis.

Another new place with Isaan Thai food, similar to the much raved about Uncle Boon's, but way better.

The food here is much more reasonably priced, with a ton more options and no silly wait times to get a table. Sure, it's not in a hip, low-lit spot in Nolita, and you instead get to step over a homeless guy or two lying out front in the beautiful Alphabet City locale, but it's so worth it for some really satisfying and delicious Thai food that's different from the typical stuff in the area.

They do have some staples that you are used to seeing, like a spicy papaya salad (topped here with a salted egg) ($11) and a pretty good Thai Basil Fried Rice with a runny egg on top ($12), but there are also some other great, unique things here. The Deep Fried Chicken Thighs ($8) were excellent. The skin was incredibly crispy and the fatty dark meat was really juicy. The final dish we got that was also great was the Grilled Marinated Beef ($8) - this comes with a very generous portion of tender beef piled high, along with a few little portions of delicious sticky rice on sticks. I would have liked some more rice with this since it was so good and since they give you so much meat, so I would suggest getting a side of some more rice.

I'm never too big a fan of dessert at Thai places, and this was no exception. I think I happened to pick the worst possible choice though, with the Taro in Condensed Coconut Milk ($8). I didn't realize it would be hot, which was strike 1. Bite 1 and 2 of the mushy, gummy pieces of taro were quick strikes 2 and 3, and I was done with it. It's very rare that I don't finish a dessert, but I could not deal with another bite of this. Fill up on the excellent food here and don't bother saving room for dessert.

Where to start? I am trying to find a better word other than "underwhelmed". But I could not. So I stick with it. 

Don't get me wrong. The food was authentic (i have been to Thailand couple times; different regions, including the northeastern region - Isan). But let's not be fooled; authentic does not equal "tastes good". I am bench-marking to the food I had in Chiang Mai and to Zabb Elee, another Isan restaurant in the city. My point is, you cannot just mix all the right ingredients together and think you will make a good dish. It dose not work that way.  There are preparations need to be done properly before and during the cooking to make the magic happen, so 1+1 bigger than 2. Here, at Somtum Der, it's just not happening. Results, 1+1 smaller than 2.

These were what I had: 
Goong chae nam pa: Prawn sashimi in green chili sauce (i think ceviche would be more appropriate based on the prep and seasoning). This is the highlight of the night then it went downhill from there.

Tum Poo Plara: Green papaya salad in fermented fish sauce and pickle crab. I told the waitress and made sure the chef "made it the way you would in Thailand". For degree of spiciness, I took 5/7. Nope. Either she did not deliver the message or it was an off night for the chef. It did not deliver much heat and i don't think i taste it much of the pla ra - fermented fish sauce. Zabb Elee has better than this.

Tom Saab Kradook On: cartilage soup with lemongrass and mushrooms. I was a bit surprised to find it on the menu as cartilage was rate to see in most Thai restaurant. But it turned out to be the biggest disappointment -  there were only three pieces of  cartilage floating in the over lemongrass-y soup. The pork and the soup were not harmoniously blended together. Never order again.

Pad Thai Mum Poo: Pad thai with crab paste and crabmeat and crispy basil. it was not bad. But again nothing special to write about. i was thinking to order the chef signature stir fried seafood suki. But the waitress strongly recommended me to go for the pad thai. I usually not a fan of pad thai - many places in the city have crap pad thai, but I wanted to trust her and give it a shot. i should have stuck to my own belief. 

To add salt to the injury, the service was bad. Don't tell me it is only 8 weeks old bla bla bla. that is not an acceptable excuse. 

Since it is not in my usual hang-around hood, I would not return any time soon unless I am in the neighborhood and Zabb Elee is closed.

KenScale: 8.0/10

Somtum Der is a Thai restaurant featuring the cuisine of Isan (Northeastern Thailand) region. I love Thai food, especially anything with curry, but apparently the Isan cuisine doesn't have one. Nevertheless, I enjoyed all the food that I ordered. It had more spicy edge than the conventional Thai food that is on the sweeter side.

I sampled a variety of dishes. Tum Thai Kai Kem (spicy papaya salad with salted egg) was very refreshing, while Goong Chae Nam Pia (prawn sashimi with house special green chili sauce) overwhelmed me a little with the spice. Sa Poak Kai Tod Der (deep fried chicken thigh) and Moo Ping Kati Sod (grilled coconut milk marinated pork skewers) were both tender and flavorful, but reminded me too much of generic fried chicken and pork skewers you see in other Asian restaurants. Larb Ped (spicy minced duck salad) was also very solid, and I couldn't stop eating Pad Ki Mao Pork & Basil (spicy flat rice noodles with ground pork and crispy basil leaves). The restaurant also serves grilled sticky rice on the side in a popsicle style.

The restaurant has a full bar and a pretty casual vibe. It doesn't take reservations, but when I stepped in for early dinner before 6, I had no trouble getting a seat. There are also communal tables in the center that are suitable for a larger group. I definitely recommend this place for a different style of Thai cuisine, especially if you want more spice and variety outside of typical curry you get through Seamless.

This was a good place, but not great.

We started with the Larb Tod, which was a good way to start off.  It had a fun flavor, which was actually somewhat new to me.  I'm not sure what it was, but I know the only other time I have tasted it was at Pok Pok NY, so it brought back good memories.

We then had the catfish soup, which was probably the most disappointing.  There was almost no meat on the catfish (a lot of bones), and there was not much else to the soup.  The flavor in the soup was standard Thai soup, a little sour, but also almost a little watered down.

Finally, I also had the Kuay Tieo Pad See Eiw Talay, which was just seafood pad see ew.  The taste was spot on, but unfortunately, it looked nothing like the picture and the visuals were a bit of a turn off.  The noodles were a bit overdone and the amount of veggies and meat in the dish left something to be desired.

TL;DR  Food was alright, not great.

[Background]: 
this Isan (Northeastern Thailand cuisine) gem opened its door in EV fall 2013 (original spot in Bangkok). Be prepared to venture for some spicy dishes - both my friends and i loved the dishes but also were sort of in tears (b/c of the spice).  the service was fast. 

i love that you can order by picture - two of us shared 3 dishes and 1 dessert. (we went for healthy dishes)

[The FOOD]: 
- i always order papaya salad at thai place (we had the tum thai - original spicy papaya salad) -it does not have the normal sweet sauce and taste more natural to me. The other 2 dishes we had larb pla dook yang (spicy minced grilled catfish salad) & moo ping kati sod (grilled coconut milk marianated pork skewer). 
- the skewers are milder than other 2 dishes. 

[The Dessert]: 
-Blackjelly with fresh milk.  i dont have sweet tooth, and Somtum Der was able to provide me the perfect dessert. (i asked for less sugar)

We got the Moo Ping Kati Sod (coconut milk marinated pork skewers), Tum Thai Kai Kem (papaya salad with salted egg), and Goong Chae Nam Pla (raw prawns with green chili sauce).  All the flavors were pretty authentic.  The papaya salad was Isan style with the salted egg, we also liked the fact that the pork skewers were not dry like most places and wasn't too fatty either.  

You can't tell from walking by on the sidewalk but the atmosphere is surprisingly nice and spacious inside, high ceilings, airy, and contemporary - this is what I imagine it would be like in modern Isan.

If you like spicy, they can definitely tailor dishes to your liking.  Their menu is huge, I will have to come back again to try more of their food.

The papaya salad was fantastic. We asked for medium spicy and the smoke is still coming out of my ears so, if you like spicy food, go for it.
I had the leaf fish salad and wasn't really into it but the coconut rice was tasty and the spring rolls were more like a pastry than any thai spring rolls i've ever had, delicious.
The staff are very nice, the vibe is mello and the singha's just kept coming so, all in all, not a bad night out.

I was really hoping for Somtum Der to be a blockbuster Thai from decor to the food.  At 930 on a Saturday night the place was buzzing with barely any tables free.  As I was waiting for my dining partner to arrive, i ordered the Somtum martini. Out came out a bland and watered down faint lemongrassy water.  I sent it back and held my breath ... Out came another version, boozier and this time with little of the promised lemongrass or other flavors, flat and missing basic sweetness that was on the ingredient list, again remake... Sigh

The decor is communal, blond wood throughout, with bar seating at the front and on the sides. 

Once my patron came, the pescetarian options were limited to catfish, mackerel papaya salad and marinated sashimi-style shrimp. We got the mackerel and i had the classic papaya salad. Both were good though the papaya was a bit soggy.  Next came the marinated beef and the grilled pork skewers.  The beef was good but nothing special. The sticky rice skewers were overly gummy and virtually inedible.  The pork was more flavorful albeit a bit chewy.   Perhaps it was an off night or I didn't pick the right dishes? Some reviews raved about the fried chicken. 

If you've had Thai at the likes of Pure Thai in HK, Somtum Der felt over hyped and under delivered.

Went with high hopes for a good inexpensive thai place .

First warning sign was the dog eared laminated menus -- but we were at the bar and watched the chef freshly make papaya salads which looked great , so I still had high hopes 

We sat down were handed menus ..within seconds we were asked to order .. bad sign .. we asked for another few minutes .. but were soon asked again to order.. bad sign.. 

We ordered .. sate spring rolls , pad thai (spicy 2* out of 4) and several other dishes
we had ordered a total of 8 dishes 

Within 5-6 minutes  ALL our food arrived .. thats not even enough time to fry an egg!

Everything (except the papaya salad) is precooked 

The pad thai was so spicy it had to be sent back ... and this took about 10 - 12 minutes to come out. and actually tasted cooked to order. 

We were asked the usual annoying "everything OK" question and for a change I answered honestly 

I said everything came out far too quickly and was mostly pre cooked and not cooked to order.. I felt we were being rushed out so they could flip the table .

I was assured everything was freshly prepared and was told that I simply didnt understand .. I assured her that I did and that I know all our food was sitting in large steam pans moments before and its just dished up .

Apparently making a scene, according to my dining friends , I let it go but thought to observe  the table of 8 next to us and timed how long it would take for their food to come ..

From the moment the waiter had taken their order to the moment their table was groaning with many dishes was just over 10 minutes .. which is an IMPOSSIBLE amount of time for food to be prepared freshly for 2 people let alone a table of eight...
 let alone a reasonable amount of time to have a good night out .. we could have been in and out in about 30 -40 mins ..



Then the bill came and it seemed that the only freshly prepared dish was billed separately ... it seems the guy standing at the bar hand preparing the papaya salads with a traditional large pestle and mortar is just some sort of ruse to make you think you are having freshly prepared food ... when in fact everything is just sitting out the back pre made .

So if you want cheap pre made cafeteria style food where they are wanting you to eat and leave as soon as possible this is for you..

If youd prefer to have your appetizers first your food cooked to order, and time to enjoy dinner with your friends .. go somewhere else .

Came here with some friends and had a huge lunch. Tried the grilled catfish salad, the fried chicken, papaya salad, and the chicken soup.  All of the dishes packed a big punch of Thai flavors one expects. I'm definitely coming back here again.

Just wish they served Bloody Mary's!!! Hint hint.

I really enjoyed my meal at this restaurant, and thought I'd finally write my first Yelp review hoping to help people who are considering dining here.

Of course, everyone is entitled to their own opinion, but I'm just going to say that there are a few things that confuse me about some of the negative reviews here:

- Complaints that the fish sauce was too salty or fishy.  It's fish sauce -- "salty" and "fishy" are kind of its jam.  When fish sauce is NOT salty or fishy enough, people will complain that flavors are not authentic enough.  Go figure.  Somtum Der is very clear about which of their dishes use a "fermented" fish sauce, which has a stronger flavor.  If you want to stay on the less adventurous side, it's totally possible to identify and avoid those dishes and stay with the still-delicious regular fish sauce foods.  Maybe split ONE fermented fish somtum amongst the group just to try it because they really are quite good and very different from what you get elsewhere, so it would be a shame to leave without at least a taste.

- Complaints that the food was too spicy.  (Real) Thai food is SPICY, and Somtum Der is very upfront about the fact that they are trying to keep in line with more authentic flavors.  Mostly, what confuses me about the complaints is that "too spicy" is a very fixable problem -- both for future visits as well as your current one.  How do I know? Because I made the mistake of ordering the max spiciness level for a dish once, due to my general arrogance about spice tolerance.  Our waitress happily took the dish back when she noticed we were struggling with it, made it less spicy, and even brought us some sweetened milk to calm our tastebuds.  The next time we went back, we ordered food less spicy and it was perfect.  Problem solved, crisis averted, star rating maintained.

- Complaints that there wasn't enough meat in the pork cartilage soup.  I've had a ton of pork in my soup both times I ordered it, and I'm not saying the reviewers are lying, but maybe they've since fixed the problem.  I'm not sure how many pieces, as I did not know the amount was contested, so I did not count.  Next time.

- The general tone of reviews, always, but that is not a somtum der thing.  That's just well, because Yelp.

Overall, my favorite dishes are the somtums with fermented fish sauce or salted egg, the larb ped (minced duck salad), the pork cartilage soup, and the grilled pork and coconut rice skewers. I keep forgetting to try the fried chicken because I order too much food already, but maybe next time because I'm sure I'll be back.

I always get excited about a new addition to my neighborhood, especially if it involves spicy Thai food. The ambience is nice, clean and casual. We shared the original papaya salad (we braved the level 3 spice and despite the fact that we both love spicy, this tested our limits...fortunately, there was no shortage of water). It was flavorful and delicious. We also went for the pork spring rolls and pad khee mao, which were great. I would definitely come back!

Found this place thanks to Thrillist a few weeks back. I can say that the best fried chicken I've ever had in my life was actually on the streets of Thailand. Some ghetto food vendor serving up juicy, perfectly crisped fried chicken. I haven't had chicken that good since then, until coming to Somtum Der. The fried chicken dish is the reason we came, and it totally met our expectations. Really cheap place to eat too, and the restaurant is trendy enough to bring friends/go for a chill date (although you might end up smelling like fish sauce by the end of the night).

I will definitely come back. Oh and the papaya salad is very authentic too, but people are not joking - it is authentically spicy as well.

Five stars for the food. Minus one for how slow our drinks and sides were, compared to everything else. Hopefully such kinks are only temporary. 

We came on a weekday night (and, as we found out later, the night before the NYT review was published), and it was relatively uncrowded. The space was not too bright, but not too dark. The servers are really friendly and helpful, so I doubt the slow delivery of certain orders was their fault. Anyway, on the food. The som tum which we ordered, was, to me, heavy on the fish sauce, but my companion loved it. We also had a 'pork cartilage' (really pork rib) soup, which was deliciously sour and spicy (too spicy for my spice-loving (but American-born) companion, who lapped it up as best she could, all the same). The fried chicken was as good as the other reviewers have proclaimed it to be, definitely on the re-order list. The special grilled marinated pork, which is like the fried chicken, but lightly breaded, was also good, and we really liked the sticky rice skewers that came with it (you can order it as a side). Fragrant and lightly chewy, it was easily one of my favorite bites of the night. We also ordered sides of fried noodles (really a delicious meatless order of pad thai) and vermicelli (avoid it, just a heap of boiled vermicelli).

Definitely recommended.

Somtum Der is a relatively new addition to the neighborhood, closer to Lower East Side, further away from any thai food.  This place has lots of potential, and with the New York Times on its back, it may be thrown into the spotlight, replacing Zabb Elee, which has since descended into the ranks and have been disappointing as of late.

Pros 
The food is good, they are getting blasted for service.  

SPICY MEANS SPICY.  We ordered medium and it was a bit much for the soup.  The Thais are crazy when it comes to spice.  


Cons
The servers had a very thick ascent, I was really struggling to understand and hear them the whole night.

Food comes out whenever they feel like it, there is no order.  Papaya salad came out second last.  Soup came out towards the middle of the meal.  One side of noodles came in the beginning, the other came almost after we ate all our food.  They need to work on the order of things.  While I usually tell the servers to just bring food out as they are ready, so nothing gets cold sitting in the kitchen, other places try harder in the progression of food.  They know certain things are considered appetizers and which ones are mains.

Drinks didn't come until we asked about them 20 minutes later.


Food
Fried Chicken Thigh - crispy goodness with spicy/sweet fish sauce.
Grilled Marinated Pork - delicious and crispy as well.  served with the same spicy/sweet fish sauce.  Sticky rice on a stick was fun.

Pork Cartilage Soup - this dish had really good flavors, unfortunately a medium spicy soup was too much for me to handle.  I had to wait for it to cool off a bit before actually be able to have this soup, but by then it had lost something.

Papaya Salad with Sweet Sauce - unfortunately this dish had too much fish sauce which ruined the balance of the dish.

Fried Rice Noodles - this was on the sides menu.  Basically pad thai without any meat.  This was delicious. Skip the vermicelli though.

I will definately go back and try out other dishes, hopefully they work our their kinks.  Otherwise I forsee that the NYT review will bring more customers that they can't handle and they will get blasted further.

My two friends and I came to Somtum Der for lunch on a Saturday afternoon, and found the restaurant blissfully empty (other than two occupied tables). It's an open and spacious restaurant, complete with a giant mirror on the back wall to make it seem even bigger. Once we were seated, we spent a good twenty minutes poring through the menu figuring out what we wanted to get. Every item on the menu comes with a picture, which was really helpful, and we were further aided by a list of recommended combinations of things to order. They also offer lunch combos for $10 or $12, which looked like a good deal but have limited options.

We ordered a bunch of things to try, going mainly off one of the recommended combos:
- Tum Suo Der (Der styled papaya salad with sweet chili sauce): I was really excited to try the papaya salad, their specialty, but I was sorely disappointed by this dish. The ingredients were really fresh, but it was incredibly salty and I didn't taste any sweet chili sauce.
- Tom Saab Kradook On (spicy Isan pork cartilage soup): Really flavorful and lemon-y. I enjoyed it, though beware of the giant brown chunks of ginger... I accidentally ate one (not knowing what it was) and it did not taste pleasant.
- Sa Poak Kai Tod Der (Der style deep fried chicken thigh): Hands down my favorite dish! The chicken was incredibly juicy and tender.
- Larb Moo (spicy minced pork salad): It was rather spicy, even though we ordered it mild (one pepper). It was otherwise not bad, and flavored with lots of red onion.
- Coconut rice: Soooo good. It came on a plate with a bit of coconut milk on the bottom, and was really great for balancing out salty/spicy dishes.
- Grilled sticky rice: Came on a skewer, which was interesting. It was dense and sweet, and felt almost like eating glutinous rice. Warning: this will make you really full!
- Black jelly with fresh milk: This was, interestingly, more like shaved ice with bits of jelly. It was pretty light on flavor, so a good option if you don't like sweet desserts.
- Thai tea panna cotta: The panna cotta came with condensed milk to pour on the side. It wasn't as sweet as the actual Thai tea with milk that I'd just ordered, so I think I preferred my drink more.

The service was a bit slow at times; our server stayed mostly behind the counter across the room so she was a bit hard to flag down. And while I enjoyed most of the dishes (other than the overly salty Tum Suo Der), I don't think I'd go out of my way to come back for anything other than the fried chicken and coconut rice.

I struggle, but just as some others have used the word, I will too. Underwhelming. 

You stand in line, wait 15 minutes for a table on a Saturday night. The menu looks fresh, different - like something special. 

We are seated in the bar, which is actually by the window, and because people waiting go in and out the cold December air makes it freezing. 

From the small selection of alcoholic drinks we order a Singha beer (can't go wrong with that one) and a traditional Thai drink with sweet basil. The cocktail drink is very cognac-like, not my type of drink, but it does have a weird resemblance with mojito. The drinks are served about ten minutes apart - the beer first, obviously, but why not serve them at the same time.

We order four dishes and coconut rice; spicy pork soup, fried chicken, fried pork and marinated, fried beef.

The spicy pork soup is large enouh to share. They give you nothing to pour it with, though. Natural, clean and strong flavor. Pork pieces, a lot still on the bone, is a nice touch, but the use of lemon grass is extreme.

The fried chicken is in itself just bland. Yes, moist and tender (when isn't a fried leg tender? You can't mess it up), but no real taste - put the sauce on, it helps.

The marinated beef came out as marinated pork. It has a very southern taste to it. Soul food almost. But ultimately the dish is too sweet, not as tender as could be - average.

The biggest disappointment of the four dishes is the fried pieces of pork. The look like potatoes, but I'd rather have fried potatoes. It's nothing but overpriced balony, fried to make it 'special'. This is what you don't even want to serve your dog.

If the food is great it's always easier to forgive circumstances. But the food is average or below, prices too high for what they give you, so the level of service can in no way be excused. They're slow, it's hard to get a hold of the waiter once you've put your order in.

Spice spoken here, English not so much!  We spice lovers ordered entries marked with 3 and 4 chilies.  Our friendly smiling server understood not a word (well, just the names of the dishes) and he told the kitchen "1 chili" for us Thai dilettantes. We really screwed that up!  

1 chili means a solid American-style medium heat level, strong notable levels of spice, not a total absence of chili peppers. We just almost broke a sweat, hardly needed any cold Beer Lao.  Of course we found out the 1-chili order detail only after we finally got the bill, that burst the bubble of us congratulating our foolish selves on eating 4-chili dishes like real men LOL.

Anyhow, Somtum Der served the most interesting, spicy, strongly flavored food I've had in a very long time. We avoided all the noodles and stuck to Isan specialties: Larb Moo was ground pork with slivered onions, finely chopped lemongrass and toasted rice for a delightful and unexpected crunch.  Spicy sardine salad brought the yummiest spicy red sauce over thin slices of fish and plenty of crunchy lemongrass stems, excellent.  Finally the papaya salad with fish sauce and little rock crab (Somtum Poo-Plara) was a delicious crunchy tangle of green papaya, pepper flakes and squishy (marinated?) crab legs. Each one about $10 for a small portion.

Coconut rice was delish, small mung beans mixed in, for texture I guess. Sticky rice was served wrapped in plastic, kinda tough, definitely not sweetened.  Both soaked up the sauces well, I just don't quite understand why rice is a la carte, you gotta gotta get some.

Vegetarian rating: 3 stars bcos several Somtum (papaya salads) are veg, you can also get bamboo soup, a veggie fried rice entree, and several sides.

We visited in the early afternoon, place practically empty but service was still distracted and slow, I don't understand that.  Finally found a woman server who spoke enough English to translate for us.

Check your bill - our total was correct but the bill showed somewhat random bar and food totals, really goofy, don't know what's going on there.

The "der" part of the name is a superlative, so it translates loosely to something like "Ueber Papaya Salad" :)

We just got back from visiting Thailand and saw that this place was reviewed by Pete Wells for NY Times and got a one star and since we live close by we decided to try it. It's a nice spacious setting, we ordered the larb moo salad, the papaya salad with fermented crab, fried chicken and coconut rice. We received the larb moo salad first, and it is spicy. When we were in Thailand, especially in the Issan area, the flavors were spicy but not acidic spicy to a point where I really don't want to eat it anymore. That's what happened here. It's just felt offensive to eat. We couldn't even taste the flavors of coconut rice as both of our mouths were seriously on fire. We can handle heat, but not like the acidity that puts a bad taste in your head and your mouth. We then tried the papaya salad with the fermented crab, has the heat as well, but by this time my mouth was just going nuts that I didn't really want to endure it anymore. Not sure why but when we were in Thailand, we were eating the lots of spicy food but there was just the perfect balance in every dish. Nothing was spicy to a point where we were offended by it... And the fried chicken was alright, it's not a typical fried chicken that it comes in and the flavors is a bit different than what we had tasted when we were in the Issan area.

Giving this 3 stars as I appreciate the level of authenticity with the menu however I do think the flavors need to be paid attention to more so as to achieve better balance between spicy, salty, sweet etc.
There's hot and then there's sweet Jesus save me from the ladyboy's gonorrhea hot.  They do warn you, but you don't listen.  Don't be a hero, even the rice is hot.
The food here is very good . Papaya salad (somtum) and fried chicken are super great i order both of them every time  I go. I recommend this restaurant

Good food but really BAD service.  I ordered 1 Papaya Salad. Only 3 customers 2 table that time. 20 mins later waitress came asked me what did I ordered because she wasn't sure. She also asked me to pointed in the menu which one. 

BTW, I went to that place many times and each time always have something wrong. Hard to believe!

If you hungry please think twice and I recommend to choose another place. But if you could wait for 30mins for just 1 or 2 dishes so it's totally fine. 

Eye contact might not work with staff in this place if you really to be serviced. Sort of ignorrant.

I am Thai, born and raised in Thailand. I have finally found a place that represents a real Thai cooking. They are not kidding about the spiciness which I love about this place.
We ordered a papaya salad with salted egg and a papaya salad with fermented fish. We love how they made it in front of us by using the big mortar.  It was very fresh and delicious, full of flavor from fresh Thai chilies, fish sauce and limes. 

Must try the deep fried chicken thighs. It was very crispy and the dipping sauce was just a good compliment to the dish.
The pork skewers were also very tasty should try it with sticky rice. We ordered Thai iced tea and Thai hibiscus drinks, also delicious. 

This place had the best thai food I ever had here in New York. Can't wait to go back!

From the bright photographs of every dish to the recommended combination platters, Somtum Der makes every effort to ease the Isan novice into the pungent cuisine of Thailand's northeast. Every concession, except when it comes to taste.

This outpost of a Bangkok Isan restaurant knows that people aren't here for sweet pad thai. Spice levels are variable but appropriately generally remain on the firey side. Get ready to order extra rice, Beer Lao or dishes with coconut milk on the side to cool the palette (avoid the electric neon cocktails, which resemble cast-offs from TGI Friday's in taste and appearance).

The pork kebabs, brushed with coconut milk and served with a small ball of vermicelli were probably the highlight, with the crunchy and spicy pork larb coming in a close second. 

New to me was the Thai take on ceviche, in this case grey, raw shrimp covered in equal parts chili pepper and lime. The slimy texture of the raw shrimp, combined the puckering aftertaste, wasn't something I'd order on a return trip. 

Everything else, however, hits the mark.

Walked in on a Saturday around 7 with about a 5 min wait for 2. Great Isan cuisine, with a sister location in Bangkok. We liked the salted egg on the original somtum. The larb moo and deep fried chicken thigh were good choices. I wasn't impressed by the grilled skewers. Overall, adjust downwards for spiciness cause real Thai is pretty spicy!

Kind of crappy service . The waiter splashed oily shit on my dining partner and didn't even apologize :/

Ok so Somtum Der almost killed my GF on Xmas eve: she is acutely allergic to shell fish I am not which we made clear when ordering. She cannot eat anything that has been cooked in a pan with any shellfish, she can't have any shellfish in her food at all. We ordered a chicken dish, a pork dish and I ordered shrimp Sashimi which wasn't very fresh I may add. Somehow after being instructed that her food could not be touched by the same hands or utensils that touched shellfish you guessed it she got the whammy. She woke up with hives all over her body xmas day and had to take benedryl all day long battling hives on her face, neck and back.
It was serious and she had to sit out Christmas. I may add I asked for the food to be prepared mild and it was extremely hot not even close to mild. Thanks for ignoring my wishes. I will never order from hear again, I had to take several Zantecs to relieve me of indigestion and heartburn.

So much for being explicit about her allergy to shellfish or wanting my food to be prepared mild.

SMH I want her Christmas back thanks guys NOT

D Ross

Great food... horrible service.

So my friend and I came here for dinner on a freezing cold December night.  She beat me to the restaurant, so she was seated and I can't say how long she had to wait before getting a seat.

This place has great lunch specials and authentic thai food (not your run of the mill pad thai), so it came highly recommended.

We decided to share dishes so did a beef skewer with coconut batter and another spicy grilled beef dish.  The food was great.  A perfect blend of spices and sweetness in the coconut dish that yielded fantastic food.

However, two areas where I was left extremely disappointed and that came to service.  First came with placing the order.  The waitress was extremely persistent, not even giving us 2 minutes before coming back and asking us if we were ready to order.  With an extensive menu and difficulty choosing we needed time, and so that was a bit annoying.

The second which was more irritating than the ordering process was during our meal.  Not even finished and with food on the plate, the bus boys started clearing off our table!  They didn't even ask if we were done before going for our plates.  We had to actually tell them to stop because we were not done.

After all that rushing to clear off the table, it took them ages to get us the check.  So in that case, I'm wondering what the huge rush was to begin with.

Food wise, I highly recommend this place as the flavors are unique and very authentic to the region.  However if you're seeking great service, look elsewhere for sure.

Came expecting amazing food and bad service but instead got okay food and pretty good service.

I ordered the crispy chicken thigh. Yes it was crispy but I love Korean chicken wings more. It had bones which I'm not a fan of since they're not as easy to pick out as wings are. The sauce it came with was spicy too but I liked it. It paired nicely with my coconut rice. My friend got the papaya salad which I liked better. It was more refreshing and tasty and was also spicy too but not overbearingly so.

The service was attentive and the ambience was nice. Not sure why anyone else was complaining...

3.5 stars.  The service was good and really great about answering questions and recommending dishes.  Staff is nice and attentive.  I really liked the decor and ambiance here.  Dimly lit, clean, busy on a Friday night, not at all as cramped as I had imagined.  Nice "dining music" playing in the background.  The food, however, didn't live up to my expectations, based on all the critics' praise from the restaurant's opening months.  I had the one Somtum (papaya salad) that came w/ Coconut Rice plus mackerel (which was a little sweet). It wasn't bad, but it wasn't really good either.  Food = 3 stars, +0.5 for everything else.

We were here because my mom had read about this place in a newspaper.  Familiar settings (I had eaten at the two restaurants that had occupied the property prior) but different food.

During the ordering process, I think every other question from my mom was "is it spicy?"  It's probably spicy - about 80% if the menu was spicy.  Don't get me wrong, I do like spicy foods, it's just that spicy food makes my body explode with sweat like the fountain show at the Bellagio.  (I'm delicate). 

Anyway, I'm writing this review long after the experience (at least a month) so I can't exactly tell you what we had, but we ordered just about everything non spicy on the menu with the exception of Gung Chae Nam Pla which is a marinated thai raw shrimp dish (lime, garlic and chilies).  That was one of my favorite dishes over in Thailand so I had to have it - and this place satisfied my craving for a while.

All in all a good experience.

Tasted: 12/2/13

This is the Thai food I crave.  Get the duck Larb, grilled pork skewers, and the Somtum that they are famous for.  Perfectly executed, bad ass, spicy as hell thai food.  The drinks are awesome, and the food was even better. I should have given this 4 stars because the service was nothing short of moronic, but i just loved the food too much.  It's totally irrelevant though, because I went to stuff my face with in your face, mouth-watering, crave-able Isan Thai.

I went with one other person and had 5 or 6 dishes.... then took 3 more to-go.  This is one of the better restaurants I've been to in recent memory.  Well's was right to put this in his top ten, and it makes me so happy to see that these kinds of restaurants get the attention they deserve.  I wish they delivered further uptown, but my waistline is somewhat thankful that they won't.  

DISCLAIMER: IF YOU DO NOT LIKE AUTHENTIC THAI, THIS IS NOT FOR YOU. IF YOU LIKE DELICIOUS FOOD THAT RIPS YOUR FACE OFF WITH SPICE, ACIDITY, AND A WARM EMBRACE.... LET ME INTRODUCE YOU TO SOMTUM DER.

I ASPIRE TO BE A REGULAR, AND I AM JEALOUS OF THOSE WHO ARE.

I like this place. It's a cute little restaurant that is not too fancy but chic enough to dine at while enjoying good food. Their price is reasonable with a slew of menu items to choose from and their service is great. 

When we arrived we were immediately greeted with a smile and presented with a menu -- the usual restaurant greeting.  The restaurant was cozy and illuminated well with soft lighting that made food more appealing (very important) and friends and diners more attractive. Hint, hint, a great spot for a cheap date if you know what I mean. 

I ended up ordering their Sa Poak Kai Tod Der ($8) a deep friend chicken thigh with a sweet dipping sauce. The thigh was fried nicely and the flavoring was perfect and savory while the meat was tender and moist. My only qualm is that I think this particular dish is overpriced considering they only give one thigh and not two.  

I also had their Khao Klook Ka Pi ($12) which translates to jasmine rice seasoned with fermented shrimp paste, served with shredded eggs, barbecued pork, and green mango. The portion was perfect with my dish was dancing with flavors and sweetness, exactly how life should be like. 

All around I enjoyed my evening at this restaurant. It is a great and reasonable priced spot to check out if you're just dining with friends or out wanting to go on a cheap date with someone you would like to get to know.

Came here eager to try out a spot specializing in Northern Thai Isaan food.  Tried one of the somtum (papaya salad) dishes - papaya salad with coconut rice and fish. Thought it was good, pretty spicy but not overly so, and not as spicy as what I had in Thailand.  Also had the fried chicken thigh, which was tasty - well fried lightly crispy but still moist. Sauce was ok. The seafood pad see ew noodle dish was pretty good.  Had a Thai cocktail drink (four different ones on the menu) which was quite tasty as well.  Prices are reasonable. Decor is simple and nice.  Tight spacing and going to the restroom is inconvenient (walk around the whole dining room then no where to wait (single bathroom) but in front of the kitchen door.

Service is so so.  We had to wait and then were told we could wait at the bar, which we did - but then they forgot to actually seat is - we finally asked and the hostess apologized for forgetting us.  We were then asked to promptly pay for our drinks - presented with a check at our table right after we were seated.  Seemed odd as at every other place I've been to we either pay at the bar or they ask and add to the check.  Otherwise table service was fine.

Unique dishes (Isan Thai, different from your standard super sweet yellow curry and ketchupy pad thai joints), quality food, very good service.  I had the papaya salad with mackerel and coconut milk grilled pork.  I thought portions were fair for the price, but they might not be enough for a huge appetite.  Order mild if you can't handle a lot of heat...they dishes were very spicy.  Would definitely eat here again.

Not all Thai food is created equal and this is currently 1 of my 2 favorite Thai places in the city.

For a little context, my original hometown has a huge Thai community with lots of authentic Thai food available, so I feel confident in saying that this place is ON POINT.

Somtum Der really surprised me as I believe that I had been to this same spot a few years ago when it had looked differently and possibly been called something else, and was left impressionless. Fast forward to a few years later and Somtum Der in its new recreation is REALLY good. 

My go to is the Larb Moo - minced pork salad. It's mixture of ground pork, red onion, scallions, lime juice, fish sauce, a little bit of toasted rice for texture and looooottttsss of thai chile peppers, just the way I like it. The flavors in this dish are so vibrant and explosive that I seriously think I die a little every time I eat it. For a little something extra, ask for a fried egg on top. Thank me later.

Their grilled marinated pork are also super meaty and deliciously marinated. Creativity points for serving them with 2 large grilled rice skewers as their "side of rice." 

Friends also got the Wok-Fried Seafood Suki, which was also very flavorful and I would definitely order on my own. I also spied the Pad Thai at a nearby table and though that's usually the LAST thing I'd ever order at a Thai restaurant, it looked so good that I might actually have to break that rule.

Lastly, for those complaining about spice level here, I say GTFO. Thai food is meant to be spicy. If you can't handle it, request "mild" or assume that your dish will come with a little kick by default. 

I, on the other hand, will continue to order my dishes "extra spicy, please."

P.S. I have also ordered delivery from this place too and I love that there's no order minimum and the food always arrives faster than the estimated time.

I love flavorful, spicy dishes and Somtum Der hits the spot. My favorite dishes in descending order:

1. Fried Chicken- perfectly crispy. Not your normal buttermilk fried chicken; It's BETTER
2. Grilled coconut pork skewers- Anything with coconut or coconut flavor tops my food list. Pork was tender and grilled to perfection
3. Larb Ped- I love duck and the green chilies add a kick of flavor
4.Chicken Soup with local herbs- Not sure what part of the chicken was in this soup. The group had narrowed it down to chicken butt or chicken neck. Even if you don't eat the chicken, it is a tasty soup. The dried mussels were a hidden treat. 
5. Grilled Mushroom and bell peppers in spicy sauce; mushrooms are on the top five of my favorite foods. This dish was good but is nothing to rave about compared to the other delicious items we ordered.
6. Thai Spicy papaya salad (Somtom)- We chose the spicy level of 2. Our mouths were on fire. I'm not a big fan of any kind of salad, which is why this is ranked so low.

Tried all three rices. My preference is the sticky, coconut rice. I ate a few spoonfuls as desert. 

If you're a group of 3-4 people whom love spicy food, Somtum Der is the place to go. Our group was really enjoying the Thai disco pop music. We found it kitchy and hilarious.

so so good.   portions kinda small for the prices .... but, man.  so worth it.  i would eat here every day.  in order of awesomeness, any of the namesake papaya salads, the fried chicken (showered with crispy fried garlic), grilled marinated skewers, and the duck larb.
Northern Thai at its best! Long wait but well worth it. Get the fried chicken, my favorite dish.

Wow. This was an awesome and authentic Thai experience.

The nytimes recently featured the papaya salad at Somtum Der as one of "The Best  Restaurant Dishes of 2013," so I checked out the website, and decided it looked like a different Thai experience, and I put it on the list of places I need to check out.

Well, last night, I crossed it off my list, but hopefully it wont be my last time! The food was excellent. We started with the original papaya salad (we ordered it mild, cause I was still recovering from some szechuan I had for lunch), which tasted similar to other papaya salads to me, but it was delicious. The waitress explained how we should eat it with the sticky rice (I guess she could tell that we weren't pros), and that definitely added to the experience. 

We also got the Koi Goong (boiled shrimp with herbs and rice) which was different, interesting, and recommended, but the taste was a little foreign for our palates, so ultimately we didn't like it as much.  

The last entree plate was the Nue Rong Hai Der + Khao Ji, (grilled and marinated beef). I really liked this, it tasted like nothing I know, and it came with grilled coconut sticky rice, which is basically a coconut sticky rice version of a corn dog (without the meat). The rice had a mild smoky flavor which was nicely complimented by the coconut. The complexity of flavors when paired with the mildly spicy sauce and grilled beef really made this dish stand out. 

If I had to do it again, I think I would change the original papaya salad for something more interesting (maybe the papaya salad with salted egg?), skip the Koi Goong (shrimp), and order the Nue Rong Hai Der + Khao Ji. (Of course, if and when I do go back, I'll probably try a few different entree dishes to spice things up.)

For dessert, the snow ice with syrup was killer. Even if it was about to blizzard, I highly recommend this. (Can't tell if it was bubble gum or cotton candy flavored, but it tasted like legit philly area ice house.)

This place has food from the northeast of Thailand. The fried chicken was tasty as was the sausage. The coconut pork skewers were a little sweet and not dry. The spicy minced duck salad was good and spicy. The fried rice with prawns was tasty and every dish is meant to be shared. The prices are reasonable and the service is friendly.

I always love going to eat with my friend Sumi, because he finds the best Thai places, and they're always so delicious and so, so cheap. He lived in Thailand for a long time, and so he knows the food and the language very well, which lucky for me, translates into him knowing the right spot to get an authentic Thai meal. Not only that, but he loves to tell you about all the fascinating elements of food and culture in Thailand, so the dinner is always a fun experience.

Last time I went out to eat Thai food with Sumi, we were in the Chelsea area and so went uptown to Wondee Siam, one of their multiple locations. I felt like Scarlett Johansen in Lost in Translation (my favorite movie after The Godfather), because there was no English being spoken, just a frenzy of everything Thai happening around me. The food was incredible, so I suggest trying that restaurant out as well. This time, Somtum Der yielded a significantly more modern atmosphere, but equally as delicious food. Sumi said that one mark of a good Thai restaurant is that the food will be un-apologetically spicy, just as it is in Thailand.  The menu is mostly in Thai terminology, but everyone there speaks English just fine, so you can ask a bunch of questions.

I think that the best way to go about this meal is to order up 2 or so plates per person and to share. We got fried chicken (amazing), crispy beef dishes, and another dish with beef and noodles that was incredible. Also, if you go, their Thai iced tea is amazing, as is any one of their many papaya salads. The one we got was so spicy, with bits of fried pork in it. I could make a meal of that every day.

And if you were wondering, yes, we did indulge in their $20 bottle of prosecco... it just felt right. Food and drink for days, an I mean a real feast here, and the total came to about $25 per person after tax and tip. I'll certainly be back! It's more of a 'friends' spot, super casual, etc., but an amazing one at that!
Don't know what the hype was about. Food was okay, but not worth the price. Do yourself a favor and go to Lui's a few blocks away

I am absolutely loving this new wave of northern Thai cuisine in New York City. At this point, I can safely say I've tried 95% of the city's Thai restaurants and Somtum Der definitely a welcomed addition to the roster. 

Just as a note of caution: this place is sppiiiccyyy. I'm glad I came here with two friends who can't even smell spice or else I would've gone all out and requested the spiciest they have to offered. That would've just been detrimental to my digestive system, for I would've eaten it all and DIED. 

Northern Thai is heavier in flavor and taste - more fried items, more spice. We ordered the somtum with salted egg, the spicy minced duck salad, the coconut milk marinated beef skewers, the pad thai, the prawns and the coconut rice. All the dishes were so well cooked and full of flavor. Although my friends can't eat spice, they still managed to finish a good portion of the food. 

While I enjoyed all the dishes, my favorite of the meal was the the pad thai. This was simply the best pad thai I've eaten in the US to date. While most pad thai have a certain sogginess to their noodles, Somtum's was dry, bringing out the flavors, fragrance and taste of a cook who clearly knows how to use a wok. I know, "dry" is a not-so-appetizing term, but it's not baking we're talking about here so just trust me on this one. I also highly recommend the coconut rice, which was how coconut rice should taste. This is the real deal and I promise you, you will like it :) 

On another note, I've read some reviews that found service to be slow and unresponsive but we had no particular issue in this case and I can honestly say this was one of the best Thai meals I've had.

Really good, but seriously spicy!   I've eaten at Somtum Der about 5 times over the last few months and have never had a bad meal, but also never left without my tongue being half on fire.   As a few people have pointed out, the portions aren't all that large so you'll probably want to order two dishes if you want to leave satiated.    For me, that's always meant starting with one of their papaya salads- which I've found to be universally flavorful.  I believe my favorite is the pork neck, with the meat offering a nice balance to the lime and papaya flavoring.   I probably have a moderate tolerance for spice-  I enjoy it, but usually will end up in sweats when eating highly spicy foods.  In this case, ordering the salad as mildly spicy was more than sufficient for me, but if you have a (very) high tolerance for the stuff feel free to press your luck.

After the salads I've typically gone with one of the meat dishes-- the fried chicken is especially tasty and the special marinated beef served with a nice chili sauce was a another favorite.

The restaurant has rarely been too crowded during the times I've gone and the service has consistently been solid.  The only real issue I have with Somtum Der is that I do feel like the portions are small relative to the price and would like to see more value for my money.  Having said that all in all, this is a great spot in the LES/ EV area and some of the best thai food I've had in New York.

This restaurant is not for you.

If your interest and experience in Thai food is limited to Pad Thai - this restaurant is not for you. 

If you only think of a stop light when it comes to Thai food (red, yellow, or green curries) - this restaurant is not for you.

If you only eat Thai food on a dare or based on the number of peppers on the menu - this restaurant is not for you

If you judge a restaurant based on the drinks and not the food - this restaurant is not for you.

If you're used to sharing large plates, and find small plates as offering "ridiculous portions" - this restaurant is not for you.

If you judge restaurants serving ethnic food based on how well servers speak or don't speak English or their native language - this restaurant is not for you.

If you find a meal tab of $ 30 pp as extravagant - this restaurant is not for you.

But, if you want an authentic Thai meal, can handle spicy food, and want to appreciate nuances of flavor and texture without leaving Manhattan - Somtum Der is the best option you have. Showcasing Isan cuisine that is now all the rage when it comes to Thai restaurants in the city, at Somtum Der you can get some of the best Papaya salads (Som Tums) and fried chicken in Manhattan. Two versions of the Som Tum that I've liked at the restaurant include a version with egg (Thai Kai Kem) that cuts the burn of the chillies and a more complex one (som tum poo-plara) with fermented fish sauce and (hard to the point of being inedible) miniature crabs. The fried chicken (Sa Poak Kai Tod Der) consists of juicy thigh meat encased in a crisp shell sprinkled with fried garlic and accompanied by a mild chili sauce. It's not a dish to be shared, and one to be ordered time and again besting almost all interpretations of the dish in the city.  Should you be looking for something grilled as opposed to fried, skip the boring skewers in favor of the house special grilled marinated beef (Nue Rong Hai Der and Khao Ji). The spicy salads (larb) are also a strong suite and my favorite is the one with crunchy, grilled catfish with lime and fish sauces, dried chilies, and toasted ground rice. The rice and noodles dishes may not be the strongest feature, still for something different you can try the chef's signature wok-fried seafood suki.

The range of flavors will ensure that your body movements are not limited to squirming and sweating uncomfortably at the spice level (though my lips did go numb after requesting one of the Papaya salads to be extra spicy), but in case you need to calm the taste buds end the meal with the Thai Tea Panna Cotta that comes with a small cup of condensed milk that needs to be drizzled over the dessert. While the Panna Cotta may occasionally lack the right texture, it's a fine way to end the meal with a light dessert -leaving you in the right mood to get back to yelp to rectify the injustice of an average 3.5 yelp rating. Somtum Der deserves better after doing its best to balance all the crappy Thai restaurants in the city that serve meals that range across the spectrum from "bland" to "pepper-heads only".

Most authentic Thai food I have ever had in nyc. I will be back again and again!!! We had the papaya salad with crab, fried chicken, sweet sausage, catfish soup, beef salad and skewers to share at the table. The only thing that i wasn't crazy over was the pork skewers, they weren't horrible but just no where near the quality of everything else. I also didn't like my lemongrass cocktail , but they replaced it with a wine and i was happy ;).
Love this place!!!!!

As of late, NYC has seen a wave of new Thai restaurants specializing in Isan cuisine, dishes originating from the northern region of Thailand that are associated with bold and complex flavors covering the spectrum of spicy, sweet, acidic, and savory. The original location in Bangkok just celebrated its two year anniversary, and Chef Thanaruek Laoraowirodge brought Somtum Der to NYC in the diverse neighborhood of East Village. A group of friends and I visited while the restaurant was still in its soft opening phase, curious to try what would come out of their kitchens.

First and foremost, order the restaurant's namesake: the Somtum, also known as the Papaya Salad. There's several iterations of this on the menu with varying accompanying proteins; my favorite was probably the Tom Kor Moo Yang, or papaya salad with grilled pork. The base of the papaya salad was spot on: the papaya was fresh and crisp, and the addition of the fish sauce, lime, chilies, and tomatoes rounded out the spicy and savory flavors of the dish. There was plenty of crunch, acidity, and a noticeable amount of spice in each bite, and the pork was tender and lightly seasoned. If you're a little more daring, try out the larb dishes, which feature a variety of diced proteins served in a salad style over sliced onions, chilis, lime, ground peanuts, and basil. Our table also shared an order of the Moo Ping Kati Sod, grilled pork served on skewers that had been marinated in coconut milk.

For my "main", I opted for the more familiar Pad Ki Mao. Somtum Der's version was a little different than what I was used to; there was an abundance of vegetables and ground pork, so the flat rice noodles played second fiddle. The addition of crispy basil leaves on top was a nice touch, as it gave a slightly different texture and aromatic edge to the dish. Although it was advertised as "spicy", I didn't really get much heat from the dish, especially in comparison to the somtum that I'd had prior. Nonetheless, it's a solid dish and well worth the price. I tried a few bites of the Pad Thai, which is served with crabmeat and crab paste, and although the crab flavor wasn't very prominent, it was fairly tasty.

Somtum Der's strength lies, unsurprisingly, in their somtums and larb salads, as well as a few of the other dishes that can be found across their fairly extensive menu. The service was a little shaky the night that we went, especially as dishes came out rather haphazardly and a few of the things we ordered never made it to the table (although they did show up on the bill), but hopefully that's been streamlined after a few months of service. I'd be more than happy to return, especially as it's pretty different from the typical Thai restaurant found in the city.

Holy!!!! New authentic Isan (northern Thai) addition to NYC! And it really lives up to it's name.  

Was recommended here by my Thai foodie friend who couldn't say enough good stuff about this.  Glad this popular Thai restaurant decided to open a joint here in NYC as well!  

Tried the duck larb, papaya salad, shrimp paste fried rice, pork cartilage tom yum soup. Everything was delish! Even the side order of noodle was up to per. Will def be a regular here!

From the moment I walked into this restaurant I can tell it was it was going to be a long love affair. It exudes a quite charm. A pining longingness.  A love affair that can be red hot or mild. It was going to be intense with breaks of coolness. This will be an enduring relationship.

The communal table is a casual touch and the well placed mirrors give the restaurant a sense of depth. The only unfortunate part is now the once bar has become a defunct clutter of jars, plates, napkins for storage. Only the lonely red bar stools, unoccupied as a sad reminder.

The food here is fantastic. The selection of papaya salad covers two pages. Tonight we tried the one with grilled pork neck and salted egg. I liked the mellowness, mild flavors of the salted egg with the spicy papaya. The pork neck added a crunchiness to the crispy green papaya. It was more intense and fiery hot. (We ordered spice level 3) The Isan grilled catfish soup was a hit. It went so well with the steamed rice. The catfish nice and crispy and broth full of flavors and deep hint of fish sauce. The prawn sashimi was delicate, fresh and bitingly spicy. Wonderful. To balance the heat, we ordered the Fried pork with basil and egg. 

The one downside. They have also fallen into like other Thai establishments, ordering the rice as a la cart where rice is a staple of South East Asia and should just come with the meal. But I can also understand because most people other than Asians don't understand the concept that the main is eaten with rice and everything isn't compartmentalize by food groups on a plate. So it would be wasteful. The rice that does come is a good portion. For the most part I can overlook this because of the flavorful food and friendly service.

Not your generic Thai joint. 
Nice staff, excellent flavor, unusual dishes. 
Not the place to go for a heaping pile of greasy pad thai, but my new go to spot for delicious authentic Thai food.

I haven't had Thai food in Manhattan in years. I only eat Thai at Sri Pra Phai in Queens and no, I do not order Pad Thai. 

This place is amazing. I ordered one of their spicy salads and it was incredibly delicious! It IS spicy though so order with caution, you can get it mild too. 

I sat by the bar where the salad chef does his magic. He has a large mortar and pestle at his station with jars of ingredients. Peanuts, spices, peppers, herbs, limes and pickled vegetables. He mixes, crushes and combines all the flavors together. It's spicy, tart, sweet, salty, and crunchy. Your taste buds will thank you.  You have to try it.

Whatever you get is amazing. Very good if you like spicy and traditional. All the papaya salads are awesome. I usually get the one with the ferment fish sauce and blue crab. I love the music and the decor, very relaxed feel.

Before coming to Somtum Der, I heard through friends that it was a chain, claiming "Authentic Thai-Isan Cuisine".  Although, I am no expert, I would say that that the food here is a good rendition of Thai Isan. I visited Somtum Der twice and found many hits on the menu and very few misses.

First try the namesake somtums - green papaya salad. Here, you'll find at least 8 types of somtums. We tried the spicy papaya salad with salted egg, the Isan papaya salad with field crabs and the spicy papaya salad with grilled pork. The components of the salad are fairly impressive. In each, you'll get more than a fistful of shaved green papaya, mixed with fish sauce, sugar, chilies and other ingredients. With the salted egg, you taste that component, mashed in with the fish sauce which gives it a nice pasty mouth feel. As for the field crab somtum, it was a bit disappointing as you could tell that the crabs were previously frozen, but still, biting into the crab released some pleasant gooey saltiness. Finally, if you order the grilled pork, you'll get an entire good quality and well-grilled pork cutlet (you can smell the char), chopped up into quarter-inch slices, which are put under the salad. All in all, somtums are in the $9 to $13 range, and for the Cheap Guy it's an excellent price.

The only thing to beware of with the somtums is that in many New York Thai restaurants, cooks tend to pile on the palm sugar or even white sugar. That happened once here, however, we were able to ask the staff to dial down the sugar and they did. 

We didn't try the soup as others had recommended nor any of the stir fried noodle or rice dishes. However, we tried the larb moo, a spicy pork salad, which is really Northern Thai and Nam Tok Moo which is the same grilled pork described above that is chopped up and mixed with crushed roasted rice. Both dishes were satisfying and seemed to have all the same flavor accents of the somtum. The only difference here is that you'll get more meat with your Larb dishes.

Other dishes we had were Sai Krok Isan - which are Isan sausages. They were okay but I felt they were a little lacking in that hint of sourness that you'll find in Thailand. Many people recommend the deep fried chicken thigh, and as advertised, it was as good as everyone says. The magic here is really the skin which is filled with garlic and herbs and somehow the flavor permeates that meat. It is presented here chopped up into bite-sized pieces. I've read that it is one of the best fried chicken dishes in New York. I definitely agree with that statement. We also had that grilled marinated pork, which as described above, had a nice genuine char aroma and herbal crust. I must say it was one of my most satisfying grilled pork cutlet due to the unique crust.

Finally, we had dessert. The best dessert is the Taro in Condensed Coconut Milk. This dessert consisted of doughy and chewy (mochi-like) balls, drenched in sweet coconut milk. It was so good, we even drank the milk. The next best dessert was the Black Jelly with Fresh Milk. This is really a shaved ice dish with black jelly and very satisfying. The last dessert we tried was the Thai Tea Panna Cotta. I thought the dish was passable, but at times it just felt like eating plain custard.

In summary, I would recommend Somtum Der. If you come here, try to go off the beaten path (i.e. don't order Chinese-style dishes like stir-fried noodles) Try many of the other dishes, such as the salads, grilled dishes, and appetizers to be exact. At prices ranging from $6 to $13, it is easy to share and realize that Thai food isn't all about pad thai.

This place was amazing. Had the green papaya salad with field crabs, the spicy catfish soup and the flat noodles with ground pork and crispy basil. 

The field crab salad was very, very spicy but good, especially if you're into the taste of field crabs, which I'm not sure I am. Everything else was stellar. The soup was delicious and had tons of crispy fried catfish, enoki mushrooms, and culantro. The noodles tasted like Malaysian hokien char mee only better and spicier. Even the drinks were great: I had the Thai iced tea with lemon (much better than with milk). Wife had the rosella juice, which apparently is a type of hibiscus. 

However, the star of this meal was the dessert. We shared the taro with condensed milk. This has to be one of the top three desserts I've ever eaten. The taro was soft as a cloud and was sitting in a glass of delicious condensed milk and coconut. Words cannot express how good this was. 

I've been hearing about how great regional Thai cuisine is as compared to the familiar stuff for a while now. After tasting this place, I totally get it!

For the level of spiciness, there is a choice of mild, medium and spicy. I chose medium. I must have forgotten that I can't handle spicy food very well, because medium was very spicy for me.

I ordered,

Tum Mangsavirat: Vegetarian Papaya Salad.

Yum Tra Krai Sardine: Sardines mixed with lemongrass, tomato sauce, herbs & spices in chili dressing.

Grilled Sticky Rice - Der's Style: Deliciously warm with a nice aroma of coconut. After eating a mouthful of spicy salad, it was so soothing to have the sticky rice.

The Boiled Bamboo Shoot cooked with traditional Isan Herbs is very spicy. I had to order 2 servings of grilled sticky rice to finish the dish.

The dishes arrived quickly. I liked everything, the salads were light and pungent and the warm sticky rice was a good accompaniment for the fiery salads. I had a very happy meal.

This place is an import from the original one in Siam Square, Bangkok. Keep in mind that this isn't the typical Thai take out menu that most New Yorkers are used to. For example, there are no curries on the menu. Having said that, the papaya salad is on point (which it should be given that somtum means papaya salad) and the catfish salad was great. The noodles were a bit too sweet for me but not overwhelmingly so. I'd come back if I was in the neighborhood.
Great food- gets really crowded sometimes but hey, Wiseman (was me) once said, go to distance and food will be tastier.

Two words: Chicken. Thigh. If you don't order it while you're here, you should poke your eye.

Now that I just proved that I'm a freestyle lyrical genius, Somtum Der is definitely worth a try if you like Isan Thai food.

Really good. Quite a few veggie selections. The soup was quite spicy, but we survived. The coconut w/ tapioca dessert was great. I wish they had a few more veggie selections, because we only had the noodles.

Went here for lunch and the food was excellent. The flavors felt authentic and the spice on the papaya salad was actually spicy! Other highlights include the fried chicken - which was probably the juiciest tfried chicken I've had in a long time, the coconut flavored pork on a skewer was nice and flavorful. 

My only complaint would be the menu - its a bit confusing and towards the back where they have the lunch specials, there are 'recommended pairings'.
